source_text: Παιδαριώδη δέ μοι δοκεῖ καὶ τὰ τοιαῦτα, ὅτι στρατηγὸς μὲν ἀγαθὸς καὶ πολλῶν μυριάδων ἡγησάμενος οὐδεπώποτε προὐδόθη, ἀλλ᾿ οὐδὲ λῄσταρχος πονηρὸς καὶ παμπονήρων ἄρχων, ὠφέλιμος τοῖς συνοῦσιν εἶναι δοκῶν· αὐτὸς δὲ προδοθεὶς ὑπὸ τῶν ὑπ᾿ αὐτῷ οὔτε ὡς στρατηγὸς ἦρξεν ἀγαθὸς, οὔτ᾿ ἀπατήσας τοὺς μαθητὰς κἂν τὴν ὡς πρὸς λῄσταρχον, ἵν᾿ οὕτως ὀνομάσω, εὔνοιαν ἐνεποίησε τοῖς ἀπατηθεῖσι. πολλὰς γὰρ ἄν τις εὕροι ἱστορίας περὶ στρατηγῶν προδοθέντων ὑπὸ τῶν οἰκείων καὶ λῃσταρχῶν ἁλόντων διὰ τοὺς μὴ τηρήσαντας τὰς πρὸς αὐτοὺς συνθήκας. ἀλλ᾿ ἔστω μηδένα στρατηγῶν προδεδόσθαι ἢ λῃσταρχῶν· τί τοῦτο συμβάλλεται πρὸς τὸ κατὰ Ἰησοῦ εἶναι τὸ ἕνα τῶν φοιτητῶν προδότην αὐτοῦ γεγονέναι; ἐπεὶ δὲ φιλοσοφίαν προβάλλεται ὁ Κέλσος, πυθοίμεθ᾿ ἂν αὐτοῦ ὅτι ἆρα Πλάτωνος ἦν κατηγορία τὸ μετὰ εἴκοσιν ἔτη τῆς παρ᾿ αὐτῷ ἀκροάσεως ἀποφοιτήσαντα τὸν Ἀριστοτέλη κατηγορηκέναι μὲν τοῦ περὶ τῆς ἀθανασίας τῆς ψυχῆς λόγου, Πλάτωνος δὲ „τερετίσματα“ τὰς ἰδέας ὠνομακέναι; ἔτι δὲ προσαποροῦντες καὶ τοιαῦτα λέγοιμεν ἄν· ἆρα Πλάτων οὐκέτι δυνατὸς ἦν ἐν διαλεκτικῇ οὐδ᾿ ἱκανὸς παραστῆσαι τὰ νενοημένα, ἐπεὶ ἀπεφοίτησεν αὐτοῦ Ἀριστοτέλης, καὶ παρὰ τοῦτο ψευδῆ τὰ Πλάτωνός ἐστι δόγματα; ἢ δύναται καὶ ἀληθοῦς ὄντος Πλάτωνος, ὡς ἂν λέγοιεν οἱ κατ᾿ αὐτὸν φιλοσοφοῦντες. Ἀριστοτέλης πονηρὸς καὶ ἀχάριστος πρὸς τὸν διδάσκαλον γεγονέναι; ἀλλὰ καὶ ὁ Χρύσιππος πολλαχοῦ τῶν συγγραμμάτων ἑαυτοῦ φαίνεται καθαπτόμενος Κλεάνθους, καινοτομῶν παρὰ τὰ ἐκείνῳ δεδογμένα, γενομένῳ αὐτοῦ διδασκάλῳ ἔτι νέου καὶ ἀρχὰς ἔχοντος φιλοσοφίας. καίτοι γε Ἀριστοτέλης μὲν εἴκοσιν ἔτεσι λέγεται πεφοιτηκέναι Πλάτωνι, οὐκ ὀλίγον δὲ χρόνον καὶ ὁ Χρύσιππος παρὰ τῷ Κλεάνθει πεποιῆσθαι τὰς διατριβάς· ὁ δὲ Ἰούδας παρὰ τῷ Ἰησοῦ οὐδὲ τρία διέτριψεν ἔτη. ἀπὸ δὲ τῶν γεγραμμένων ἐν τοῖς βίοις τῶν φιλοσόφων πολλὰ ἄν τις εὕροι τοιαῦτα, ἐφ᾿ οἷς ἐγκαλεῖ τῷ Ἰησοῦ διὰ τὸν Ἰούδαν ὁ Κέλσος. οἱ δὲ Πυθαγόρειοι κενοτάφια ᾠκοδόμουν τοῖς μετὰ τὸ προτραπῆναι ἐπὶ φιλοσοφίαν παλινδρομήσασιν ἐπὶ τὸν ἰδιωτικὸν βίον· καὶ οὐ παρὰ τοῦτο ἀσθενὴς ἦν λόγῳ καὶ ἀποδείξεσι Πυθαγόρας καὶ οἱ ἀπ᾿ αὐτοῦ.
pass_a_gloss: Childish (παιδαριώδης) to me seem also such things, that a good general (στρατηγός), having led (ἡγέομαι) many myriads (μυριάς), was never yet betrayed (προδίδωμι), nor even a wicked (πονηρός) robber chief (λῄσταρχος) and ruler (ἄρχων) of utter villains (παμπόνηρος), seeming to be useful (ὠφέλιμος) to those with him (οἱ συνόντες); but he, betrayed by those under him, neither ruled (ἄρχω) as a good general, nor having deceived (ἀπατάω) the disciples did he instil (ἐμποιέω) in the deceived even the goodwill (εὔνοια), so to name it, as toward a robber chief. For one could find many histories (ἱστορία) about generals betrayed by their own (οἰκεῖοι) and robber chiefs caught (ἁλίσκομαι) because of those not keeping (τηρέω) the compacts (συνθήκη) toward them. But let it be that none of generals or robber chiefs was betrayed; what does this contribute (συμβάλλομαι) toward its being against Jesus that one of his pupils (φοιτητής) became his betrayer (προδότης)? Since Celsus puts forward (προβάλλομαι) philosophy (φιλοσοφία), we would inquire of him whether it was an accusation (κατηγορία) of Plato that Aristotle, having departed (ἀποφοιτάω) after twenty years of hearing (ἀκρόασις) him, accused (κατηγορέω) the doctrine (λόγος) about the immortality (ἀθανασία) of the soul and named Plato’s Ideas (ἰδέαι) 'twitterings (τερέτισμα)'? Further raising difficulties (προσαπορέω) we would say such things: was Plato no longer capable (δυνατός) in dialectic (διαλεκτική) nor sufficient (ἱκανός) to establish (παρίστημι) what he had thought (νοέω), since Aristotle departed from him, and on this account are Plato’s doctrines (δόγματα) false (ψευδής)? Or is it possible, Plato also being true (ἀληθής), as those philosophising according to him would say, that Aristotle became wicked and ungrateful (ἀχάριστος) toward the teacher? But also Chrysippus in many places of his writings (σύγγραμμα) appears attacking (καθάπτομαι) Cleanthes, innovating (καινοτομέω) against the things held (δοκέω) by him, who had become his teacher while he was still young (νέος) and having beginnings (ἀρχαί) of philosophy. And indeed Aristotle is said to have attended (φοιτάω) Plato twenty years, and Chrysippus too to have made his studies (διατριβή) with Cleanthes no little time; but Judas did not spend (διατρίβω) even three years with Jesus. From things written in the lives (βίοι) of the philosophers one could find many such things, on which Celsus accuses (ἐγκαλέω) Jesus because of Judas. The Pythagoreans built (οἰκοδομέω) cenotaphs (κενοτάφιον) for those who after being turned (προτρέπω) to philosophy ran back (παλινδρομέω) to the private/lay life (ἰδιωτικὸς βίος); and not on this account was Pythagoras weak (ἀσθενής) in reason (λόγος) and demonstrations (ἀπόδειξις), and those from him.
pass_b_english: Childish, too, seem to me such claims as this: that “a good general, who has led many tens of thousands, has never been betrayed; no, nor even a wicked robber chief, captain of utter villains, since he seemed useful to those with him. But he, betrayed by those under him, neither led them as a good general, nor, after deceiving his disciples, did he inspire in those he had deceived even the goodwill, if I may call it so, that men feel toward a robber chief.” For one could find many accounts of generals betrayed by their own people, and of robber chiefs captured because of men who did not keep their agreements with them. But let it be granted that no general or robber chief was ever betrayed: what does this contribute toward making it a point against Jesus that one of his pupils became his betrayer?

Since Celsus professes philosophy, we would ask him: was it a charge against Plato that Aristotle, after hearing him for twenty years, left him and attacked his teaching on the immortality of the soul, and called Plato’s Ideas “twitterings” (Aristotle, Posterior Analytics 1.22, 83a33)? We might press the difficulty further and say: was Plato no longer strong in dialectic, or able to establish what he had thought out, once Aristotle had left him, and are Plato’s doctrines false for that reason? Or is it possible that, while Plato was right, as those who follow his philosophy would say, Aristotle proved wicked and ungrateful toward his teacher?

Chrysippus, too, is plainly attacking Cleanthes in many places in his writings, bringing in new views against what Cleanthes had taught, though Cleanthes had been his teacher when Chrysippus was still young and only beginning in philosophy. Yet Aristotle is said to have studied with Plato for twenty years, and Chrysippus to have spent no short time with Cleanthes; but Judas did not spend even three years with Jesus. From what is written in the lives of the philosophers one could find many things like those for which Celsus blames Jesus on account of Judas. The Pythagoreans used to build empty tombs for those who, after being turned to philosophy, ran back to ordinary life; and Pythagoras and his followers were not, for that reason, weak in argument and proof.

choices.term: τί τοῦτο συμβάλλεται πρὸς τὸ κατὰ Ἰησοῦ εἶναι
choices.why: τί τοῦτο συμβάλλεται πρὸς τὸ κατὰ Ἰησοῦ εἶναι ...: 'contribute to the case against Jesus' tightened to 'contribute toward making it a point against Jesus', matching the Greek construction
φιλοσοφίαν προβάλλεται: 'makes a show of philosophy' implied pretence the Greek does not say; now 'professes philosophy'
καὶ ἀληθοῦς ὄντος Πλάτωνος: concessive restored ('while Plato was right ... Aristotle proved wicked'), not two parallel claims

καινοτομῶν παρὰ τὰ ἐκείνῳ δεδογμένα: 'breaking with his teachings' changed to 'bringing in new views against what Cleanthes had taught'; φαίνεται + participle as 'is plainly attacking'; ambiguous 'he' made 'Chrysippus'
checked: Aristotle, Posterior Analytics 1.22, 83a33 (τερετίσματα) is the right source; Celsus's general/robber-chief argument stays in quotation marks; no Scripture in this chapter

anf_compare.notes: Crombie (ANF 1872) and Chadwick (1953) were not used or consulted; English is from the Greek.

translator_notes: No Scripture in this chapter. The general/robber-chief argument is Celsus’s Jew’s, reported by Origen with ὅτι and set in quotation marks as his; the phrase ἵν᾿ οὕτως ὀνομάσω (‘if I may call it so’) could be Origen’s own aside (he uses it often) rather than Celsus’s, but it sits inside the reported argument and is kept there. ‘Twitterings’ (τερετίσματα): Aristotle, Posterior Analytics 1.22, 83a33 (τὰ γὰρ εἴδη χαιρέτω· τερετίσματά τε γάρ ἐστι). Aristotle’s twenty years with Plato and Chrysippus’s studies under Cleanthes are standard biographical tradition (compare Diogenes Laertius 5.9; 7.179), not cited inline since Origen quotes no text; ‘the lives of the philosophers’ is kept lower-case as a general reference, not certainly Diogenes Laertius’s book. The Pythagorean cenotaphs for lapsed members are also reported by Iamblichus, Life of Pythagoras 73, and Origen returns to them in Against Celsus 3.51; not cited inline. ‘Ordinary life’ renders ἰδιωτικὸν βίον (the life of a layman, outside philosophy). ‘Not even three years’ reflects the Gospel chronology of Jesus’ ministry; no single verse cited.
